title: The temple falls (AD 70)
hookLine: Rome destroys the temple, and both Judaism and Christianity must learn to live without it
carry: pray for the peace of jerusalem

cards: Walking out of the temple in Jerusalem, the rebuilt temple that stood where the old one burned, a disciple turns to Jesus, full of awe: "Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!"
And Jesus answers: "Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down." In Mark's Gospel, it's said in passing, on the way out.
Years later, Roman armies put down a revolt in Judaea, and the temple burns. Jews and Christians both have to answer the same question: now what?

teach.h: HE BEHELD THE CITY, AND WEPT.
teach.b: Start with grief, because the texts do. Luke says that when Jesus came near the city, "he beheld the city, and wept over it." He wept for Jerusalem, not against it.
The temple was the center of Jewish worship: sacrifice, festivals, priests. For the first Christians it was their temple too; Acts shows the apostles praying there day after day.
When it fell, both communities had to find how God is worshiped without it. Jewish tradition tells of teachers who rebuilt Judaism around prayer, study and the home.
A rabbinic story remembers a teacher walking past the ruins with a student who mourns that the place of atonement is gone.

The teacher says there is another atonement as good, deeds of loving-kindness, and he quotes the prophet Hosea: "For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice." Christians know that verse too; in Matthew, Jesus quotes it twice.
Jews still mourn the temple on a fast day, Tisha B'Av, and at a Jewish wedding, tradition breaks a glass to remember Jerusalem in the middle of joy. Christians spoke of a temple that couldn't burn.

teach.h: YE ARE THE TEMPLE OF GOD.
teach.b: John says that when Jesus said destroy this temple, "he spake of the temple of his body." And Paul writes to Corinth: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?"
Two faiths, one loss, and some shared verses to carry it.

teach.h: PRAY FOR THE PEACE OF JERUSALEM.
teach.b: And the city is still prayed for, in a psalm Jews and Christians both sing: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee."

how: Christians pray for Jerusalem with the words of Psalm 122, and the fall of the temple is read in churches from the Gospels, where Jesus foretells it and weeps over the city.

games.q: the temple falls — tap the pairs.
p: ye are the temple of God

s: in Luke, Jesus looks at Jerusalem and passes by without a word
Luke 19:41: he beheld the city, and wept over it.
the first Christians prayed at the temple
Acts shows the apostles there day after day.
Hosea's line about mercy, not sacrifice, belongs to one faith only
it's Hebrew scripture, remembered in Jewish tradition and quoted by Jesus in Matthew.

games.q: you're a teacher walking past the ruins of the temple. your student says, the place where our sins were atoned is gone. what do you answer?
o: we must rebuild it before we can worship again.
there's another atonement: deeds of loving-kindness.
then there's nothing left to do.
games.why: a rabbinic story gives that answer and quotes Hosea: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice. Jesus quotes the same verse in Matthew.

practice: Bring to mind the city as it is today: Jews at the Western Wall, Christians in the old churches, Muslims at their mosque, families in ordinary streets, people who are afraid, and hold all of them without taking a side.
If you pray, say the psalm's own line slowly a few times, pray for the peace of Jerusalem; if you don't, hold the city in your attention and wish it peace.

wordCard.voice: Hosea. The prophet whose words, I desired mercy, and not sacrifice, a teacher used to console a student grieving the fallen temple.
